13.22.2.en: Spiritually, he points here to the poor who are bound to work long hours to support their families, and yet insist on devoting some times, however brief, to worship, remembering the name of God and offering constant sacrifices of thanksgiving all day long; so they receive abundant spiritual food, while some of the rich make the excuse that they have no time for worship. They excuse themselves by saying there is no time for God, and in truth they have not a heart consecrated to God!

13.22.3.en: * Remember that St. Basil the Great answered the question, how could the Apostles pray without ceasing? He said that in everything they did they thought of God, living in constant consecration to God. This spiritual state was their unceasing prayer.

13.23.0.en: Fr. Theophan the Recluse "He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him seeketh chastening for him." [24]

13.23.1.en: Lack of discipline is not love or tenderness toward children, but a lack of love, for parents who ignore the discipline of their children are preparing them for failure and bitterness. This is what Eli the priest fell into. For the Lord said to Samuel: "I have told him that I will judge his house for ever for the iniquity which he knoweth; because his sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not. And therefore I have sworn unto the house of Eli, that the iniquity of Eli's house shall not be purged with sacrifice nor offering for ever" (1 Sam 12:3-14).

13.23.2.en: * Do not be afraid to rebuke them and to teach them wisdom firmly, for your discipline does not kill them, but rather preserves them... He who neglects to counsel and teach his son hates him.

13.23.3.en: The Canons of the Apostles * The correction of a son by his father, who does not spare his rod, is profitable, to bring the son's soul back to obedience to the commandments of salvation. He disciplines with a rod, as we read: [I will visit their transgressions with a rod] (cf. Ps 89:32).

13.23.4.en: St. Ambrose * The corruption of children does not come from nothing, but from the madness that seizes fathers regarding earthly concerns. Concern for earthly things alone, and regarding everything else as of no value, drives them involuntarily to neglect the souls of their children. I say that these fathers (and let no one think that these words are born in me from anger) are worse than the murderers of children. The first separates the body from the soul, but the other casts both together into the fires of Gehenna. Death is inevitable according to the natural order, but the second fate fathers could avoid, if the neglect of fathers did not lead to it. Bodily death can end in a moment by the resurrection when it comes, but there is no reward awaiting the lost soul. It does not enjoy the resurrection, but suffers eternal pains. This means that it is not unjust to call such fathers worse than the murderers of children. It is not so cruel to sharpen a sword and hold it in the right hand to plunge it into the heart of a child as it is to shatter the soul and humble it, for there is nothing equal to the soul.

13.24.0.en: "The righteous eateth to the satisfying of his soul: but the belly of the wicked shall want." [25]

13.24.1.en: The righteous may eat little food, but he eats with joy and gladness of heart, for what occupies him is not the pleasure of taste, but thanksgiving to God, who gives him the food and grants him life. But the wicked is never satisfied; whenever he eats he asks for more, even if his stomach is full, for there is no satisfaction in his depths.

13.24.2.en: In the parable of Lazarus and the rich man, the rich man fared sumptuously every day, yet asked for more, and after leaving the world he longed that Abraham would send poor Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his tongue, for he was tormented in the flame (Lk 16:14).

13.24.3.en: * "And ye shall eat your bread to the full" (Lev 26:5): I do not reckon this to concern a material blessing, as if the man who keeps the law of God will receive that common bread in abundance. Why not? Do not wicked sinners also eat bread, not only in abundance, but also in luxury and ease? Therefore let us rather look to Him who says: "I am the living bread which came down from heaven" (Jn 6:51), "if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever" (Jn 6:51). Since we observe that He who said this is the Word on whom the soul feeds, we realize what bread this is of which God says in the blessing: "Ye shall eat your bread to the full." Solomon declares something similar concerning the righteous, when he says in the Book of Proverbs: "The righteous eateth to satisfy his soul: but the souls of the wicked shall want." If this were understood only literally it would seem vain, for the souls of the wicked eat with the greatest greed, and struggle to be satisfied, while the righteous sometimes hunger. Finally, Paul was a righteous man and said: "Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted" (1 Cor 4:11), and also says: "In hunger and thirst, in fastings often" (2 Cor 11:27). How then does Solomon say that the righteous eats to satisfy his soul?

13.24.4.en: Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles St. Clement of Alexandria relied on scriptural phrases, especially from the Book of Proverbs (13:5; 17:15, 23:3; 24:41-44), to give a living picture of the conduct of the Christian concerning food, and for that reason in his book "The Instructor," Book 2, ch. 1, it is said: 1. Food is not a goal we desire, but a means of life, so the word of God leads us not to the lust for food, but to the enjoyment of eternity.

13.24.5.en: [Food is not to be our chief concern, nor our pleasure and goal in life, but a means for our life which the Lord, the "Word," arranges to lead us to eternity.]

13.24.6.en: [They did not realize that God gave His creature man food and drink so that he might live and continue in life, and not for pleasure.]

13.24.7.en: [We were created not to eat and drink, but to devote ourselves to the knowledge of God... For the wicked belly is never satisfied (Prov 13:25), since it is filled with an appetite that is neither satisfied nor quenched.] 2. Let everything be in moderation, so let us not seek exaggerated, appetizing foods, but simple food that is easily digested.

13.24.8.en: [We must have a kind of discernment concerning food, so that the food is simple, very ordinary, suited to simple children... It paves the way for a life based on two essentials, health and strength. This accords with food's being simple and uncomplicated, so that it is easy to digest, makes the body light and nimble, and brings about growth and health.]

13.24.9.en: [The wretched art of cookery spoils the taste, as happens in the art of making sweets and pastries.]

13.24.10.en: [The human body gains no benefit from extravagance in kinds of food; on the contrary, those who use the minimum of food are stronger, healthier and more honorable and esteemed; we see servants healthier than their masters, and farmers sounder in body than landowners.] 3. Moderate food supports man in his mental ability.

13.24.11.en: [Philosophers are wiser than the rich, because they do not bury the mind under heaps of food, nor deceive themselves with pleasures and delights, but the love-feast "agape" `agapy is in the heavenly food, and in the feast of the mind and sound thinking.]

13.24.12.en: [The glutton is like one who buries his mind in his belly.] 4. Occupation with the heavenly food that satisfies the needs of the soul:

13.24.13.en: [The Holy Bible says: "Be not desirous of dainties: for they are bread of lies" (Prov 23:3), because they belong to a kind of false and base life, for they give their attention to luxurious dishes of food, whose fate a little later is to be thrown into the drain. But those who seek the heavenly food that remains must subdue the lusts of the belly, which are of a far lower rank than heavenly things.]

13.24.14.en: [Truly it is admirable to lift our eyes upward, to what is true and real... so that we taste and enjoy what is of true gladness and pure joy. For this is true love (agape); this is the food that comes from Christ and in which it is fitting for us to share.]

13.24.15.en: [The true and real food is thanksgiving to God; he who offers thanks and praise to God does not occupy himself with pleasures and delights.

13.24.16.en: If we wish to encourage our fellow guests to walk in virtue, we must keep away from rich, luxurious dishes (when we entertain them), and show ourselves clear, shining examples of virtue... and so gain a man for Christ by a little self-control.]

13.24.17.en: * We were created not to eat and drink, but to attain to the knowledge of God. The Holy Bible says: "The righteous eateth to satisfy his soul, but the belly of the wicked is always in want," hungry continually in a greed that cannot be restrained.

13.24.18.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * We must reckon the food promised in the Law to be the food of the soul, which does not satisfy both elements of man's nature but the soul alone. The words of the Gospel, though they may contain a deep meaning, can also be understood in their plain and simple sense, for they teach us not to be anxious and troubled about our food and clothing, but, living in simplicity and asking only for what is necessary, to put our trust in God's providence.

13.24.19.en: Origen Origen sees that this phrase cannot be interpreted literally but spiritually, for many of the righteous go hungry and are in need, while the bellies of the wicked are filled with food and drink. The Apostle Paul says: "Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace" (1 Cor 4:11), and he says: "In hunger and thirst, in fastings often" (2 Cor 11:27). What the wise Solomon says concerns another food, which is the word of God and His wisdom, from which the soul of the righteous is satisfied.

13.24.20.en: * We too are nourished by the word that satisfies our souls, for it is written "The righteous eateth to the satisfying of his soul" (Prov 13:25), and from the kind of food by which we are nourished nothing proceeds but good speech and no other.

13.24.22.en: From Your hands I receive discipline,

14.0.s.en: 1. The wise woman and the foolish woman

14.0.0.en: 1 The wisdom of woman buildeth her house: but folly plucketh it down with her hand.

14.0.1.en: The wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hand [1].

14.0.2.en: If the modern world is much concerned with the rights of women, this concern is the offspring of living Gospel thought, although what occupies many is material and formal rights. But the Holy Bible, in both Testaments, looks upon woman, whether as wife, mother or sister, as the backbone of the family, with a strong effect on the rest of the family members, and on creating an atmosphere of love, family warmth and unity.

14.0.3.en: It is within a woman's power to build her house and within her power to pull it down; not by beauty of body nor by material means does a woman establish her house, but by wisdom, as by ignorance and folly she pulls it down. If she carries her Christ, the wisdom of God, within her, she draws her husband and children to Him, and her house grows into a holy, rejoicing church; but if she walks outside Christ and lives for the pleasures of the world, she brings her house down to the pit.

14.0.4.en: Through the holy life, wise in the Lord, the Church, like the human soul, builds her heavenly dwelling by divine grace, but the wicked soul pulls down with her own hand the glory prepared for believers, that is, by her wicked life, unseemly conduct and rebellion.

14.0.5.en: * It is written: "Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands" (Prov 14:1). This means that the wise woman encourages her neighbor in the fear of the Lord, and the love in her heart toward her sister and sisters. But on the other hand the foolish woman breaks down with her words full of bitterness, hatred, evil and contempt, as it is written: "In the mouth of the foolish is a rod of pride: but the lips of the wise shall preserve them" (cf. Prov 14:3).

14.0.6.en: St. Wissa * Here [the meeting of the Lord Christ with the Samaritan woman (Jn 4)] a woman proclaimed Christ to the Samaritans, and at the end of the Gospels also a woman who saw Him before all the others tells the Apostles of the Savior's resurrection (Jn 20:18).

14.0.7.en: Origen * "Every wise woman buildeth her house." The Church builds her house by her patience and her hope in Christ, that is, she raises up and corrects those who enter her by her teaching and her faith. "The foolish plucketh it down with her hands." This is heresy, which becomes the cause of their eternal death.

14.0.8.en: * In speaking of the glory of man, Paul now establishes a balance, so that the man should not boast beyond what is fitting, nor the woman be pressed down. For in the Lord the woman is not independent of the man, nor the man independent of the woman. If you ask who came after the other, each is the cause of the other, or rather each is not from the other, but God is the cause of all.

14.0.9.en: * The women stood at the Cross, the weaker sex that appeared stronger, and so everything changed completely.

14.0.10.en: St. John Chrysostom * Virtue is one in man and woman, since their creation was surrounded with equal honor. Hear the Book of Genesis: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them" (Gen 1:27). Since their nature is one and they have the same actions, their rewards must also be the same.

14.0.11.en: St. Basil the Great * She who was formerly a servant of death has now been freed from her crime by serving as the voice of the holy angels, and by being the first preacher of the news concerning the joyful mystery of the resurrection.

14.1.0.en: He that walketh in his uprightness feareth the LORD: but he that is perverse in his ways despiseth him. [2]

14.1.1.en: Our Lord Jesus says: "I am the way" (Jn 14:6), and He is the goal to which we come. Both uprightness in the way and deviation from it are bound up with our relationship with Him. If we abide in Him and He in us, we walk the royal road, and if we ignore Him in our lives we deviate from the way as from achieving the goal.

14.1.2.en: He who is upright in his way bears a divine fear (godliness in the Lord) that supports him, so that he does not turn to the right hand or to the left, meaning that he does not fall into evils, nor boast proudly like the proud. But he who walks crookedly off the royal road makes light of God and does not fear the final judgment.

14.1.3.en: Walk with Him, and you will reach God. By Him you walk, and to Him you go.

14.1.4.en: Do not look to any other way by which to go to Him.

14.1.5.en: Had He not by His grace consented to become the Way, we should have remained in perpetual wandering.

14.1.6.en: I do not tell you to look for the way, for the Way itself has come to you; arise; walk.

14.1.7.en: * Beloved, the end of all roads is Christ; in Him we become perfect, for our perfection is to return to our home in Him.

14.1.8.en: Seek nothing else besides Him. He is your goal, and to Him you are journeying, and when you reach Him do not seek anything else. For you cannot desire anything better than to have your home in Him.

14.1.9.en: He leads us by being Himself our way, and draws us to Himself by being our home. We come through Christ to Christ, through the Word who became flesh, to the Word who in the beginning was God and was with God, for He says: "I am the way, and to me you come."

14.1.10.en: St. Augustine * "He that walketh in his uprightness feareth the LORD." Not every fear makes men walk uprightly, but the fear of the Lord... The life supported by virtue is very famous, but adding the fear of the Lord to it makes persons more godly.

14.1.11.en: * "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (Jn 6:14).

14.1.12.en: If I am the Way, you do not need anyone to hold your hands...

14.1.13.en: He says: "If I am the only authority who brings to the Father, you certainly come to Him, for you cannot come by another way."

14.1.14.en: St. John Chrysostom * Isaiah says: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of them that bring good tidings" (Isa 52:7). He sees how beautiful and fitting is the proclamation of the Apostles who have walked (in Christ), He who said: "I am the way" (Jn 14:6). He praises the feet of those who walk in the way, who think on Jesus Christ, and go through this door to God (the Father).

14.1.15.en: They proclaim good things, the beautiful feet, that is, Jesus.

14.2.0.en: "In the mouth of the foolish is a rod of pride: but the lips of the wise shall preserve them." [3]

14.2.1.en: The mouth of the fool is a throne on which sits an arrogant king who commands and forbids, seeking what is for his own honor and not what is for the good of others; but the wise man's lips bring forth building words that preserve him and support him.

14.2.2.en: A man's mouth judges him; the fool judges himself by himself through the words that come from his mouth and issue from the pride of his heart. But the wise man is witnessed to by his gentle words, full of the truth that is not separate from the love in his heart. The wise man in his long-suffering meets wrath with a soft answer and turns it away; his judgments are true because he is slow to speak and swift to hear.

14.2.3.en: In pride and haste Goliath the giant said to David the young boy: "Come to me, and I will give thy flesh unto the fowls of the air, and to the beasts of the field" (1 Sam 17:44). But David, in humility with faith in the power of God, said to him: "Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied" (1 Sam 17:45).

14.2.4.en: * What judgment is harsher than that which issues from our hearts, in which each stands convinced and accuses himself of the harm caused by a fault against his brother? This is what the Holy Scriptures speak of quite clearly, saying: "In the mouth of the foolish is a rod of iniquity"; so folly is condemned as it causes iniquity. Should we not avoid this more than death, or loss, or want, or captivity, or sickness? Who does not count a bodily defect or the loss of an inheritance as far less than some defects of the soul and the loss of reputation?

14.3.0.en: 4 Where no oxen are, the crib is empty: and much increase is by the strength of the ox.

14.3.1.en: "Where no oxen are, the crib is clean: but much increase is by the strength of the ox." [4]

14.3.2.en: Where there are no oxen the crib is clean but of no use; but he who has a strong ox puts in much produce and the crib needs cleaning. So he who does not work does not err, but he gains no experience and has no fruit; but he who serves and works errs and learns from his error and gains experience.

14.3.3.en: This proverb directs our attention to the danger of rashness in our dealing with those who err. It is not fitting to kill an ox because it makes the crib unclean. Truly by killing it the aim is achieved, which is that the crib remains clean, but the man loses his ox that is useful to him in farming. Many are hasty in seeking the purity of the Church by searching out the erring in haste and rashness, and without long-suffering.

14.3.4.en: If God cares even for oxen, commanding us not to muzzle their mouths (1 Cor 9:9), how much more is it fitting for us to care for our brothers, and not to stifle their breath without listening to them and conversing with them.

14.3.5.en: St. Ambrose wrote two letters. The first he addressed to the followers of Novatian, who refused to accept the repentance of those who denied the faith through fear of torments, or of others who had committed sins which in their view allowed no repentance. It is a letter that reveals to all of us how great God's love for sinners is, how He opens the doors of hope without limit, how easy is the way of repentance and returning to God, and our obligation to be long-suffering with them until we win them to the Kingdom of God. The second he addressed to us sinners, lest we make light of God's mercies and turn the hope of repentance into an opportunity for slackness and postponement.

14.3.6.en: * Gentleness is an imitation of heaven's tenderness toward men, aiming at the salvation of all, seeking this end by a means that men's ears can bear, without their hearts failing or their souls despairing.

14.3.7.en: He on whose shoulders the correction of human weaknesses has been laid must bear them and not cast them off, even if they weigh down his shoulders, for the Holy Bible says of the shepherd that he carries the lost sheep and does not cast it off... For how shall he come forward to you whom you despise, he who will find himself an object of the rebuke of his physician, instead of being an object of his sympathy?!

14.3.8.en: Jesus had compassion on us so as not to make us fear Him, but to call us to Himself. He came in meekness, in humility... and thus He said: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mt 11:28). And thus the Lord refreshed us and did not shut us out or drive us away.

14.3.9.en: And in choosing the disciples, He chose those who would interpret His will, who gather the people of God without scattering them. Those who run after harsh, arrogant opinions, and are not gentle and meek, are not counted among the disciples of the Lord. These, while they seek for themselves the mercies of God, deny them to others. Such are the teachers of the heresy of Novatian, who count themselves righteous...

14.3.10.en: What cruelty is worse than to punish others without mercy, and to refuse forgiveness to those whom they urge to accept discipline and repentance?!

14.3.11.en: * We must know that God is a God of mercy, inclined to pardon and not to harshness. Therefore it is said: "I desired mercy, and not sacrifice" (Hos 6:6); how then does God accept your offerings, you who deny mercy, when it is said of God that He has no pleasure in the death of the sinner as much as that he return (Ezek 18:32)?!

14.4.s.en: 5. The faithful witness and the false witness

14.4.0.en: "A faithful witness will not lie: but a false witness will utter lies." [5]

14.4.1.en: Our calling is to follow Him who is in truth "the Amen, the faithful and true witness" (Rev 3:14).

14.4.2.en: The Canons of the Apostles see in this phrase a picture of the true martyrs who hold fast to the truth and will not lie, offering their blood as a living witness to the true faith.

14.4.3.en: So it is fitting for us, as we abide in the faithful witness, to be witnesses of truth to the Gospel of Christ, speaking the truth, and allowing lying no place in us.

14.4.4.en: The Holy Bible commands us to testify to the truth, and not to be false witnesses: "Thou shalt not receive a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness" (Ex 23:1). It also requires us not to remain silent before a false witness against someone when we know the truth, but to testify in order to save him: "And if a soul sin, and hear the voice of swearing, and is a witness, whether he hath seen or known of it; if he do not utter it, then he shall bear his iniquity" (Lev 5:1).

14.4.5.en: * The witness of Christ is established in us if we can say like the Apostle Paul: "For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Rom 8:38-39). But if we are troubled by the most trivial things that happen, the witness of Christ is not fully established in us.

14.4.6.en: Origen * False swearing and lying are both punished by divine judgment, and as the Scripture says: "The mouth that lieth slayeth the soul" (Wis 1:11). He who speaks the truth swears, for it is written: "A faithful witness will not lie" (Prov 14:5).

14.5.0.en: "A scorner seeketh wisdom, and findeth it not: but knowledge is easy unto him that understandeth." [6]

14.5.1.en: The man who mocks his brother or scoffs at the salvation of his soul and the salvation of his brothers has no place for the fear of the Lord in his heart. He may seek truth and wisdom with his tongue, but his heart and mind care nothing about the answer. For this reason he will not be wise even if he pursues wisdom, for it will not dwell in a heart that is neither loving nor earnest; but he who understands things, and realizes his role in life, in earnestness, knowledge is not far from him; its way is easy for him.

14.5.2.en: The mocking man finds in the word of God no fountain of life to enjoy, but mocks even the word of God, and criticizes it, and even stumbles at the person of the Lord Christ, the Savior of the world. As the Lord Christ Himself said: "If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloke for their sin" (Jn 15:22). And it was said of the Lord Christ: "Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed" (Rom 9:33). "We preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness" (1 Cor 1:23).

14.5.3.en: * Men stumble when they stop thinking about where they are going, and look to other things. This is what happened with the Jews, for they were occupied with matters outside the Law, and so did not perceive the stone of which the prophets prophesied.

14.6.0.en: "Go from the presence of a foolish man, when thou perceivest not in him the lips of knowledge." [7]

14.6.1.en: Let a man flee from the presence of the fool who does not speak words of knowledge, as one flees from his enemy, for he causes troubles and harms those around him.

14.6.2.en: The Christian man realizes the value of every second of his life, so with his love for all mankind he does not allow himself to waste his time in friendship with foolish wicked men, who see life as a sport of no value. And in leaving their friendship he neither despises them nor despairs of their salvation, but spends in love all he can for their edification, but not at the expense of his own soul.

14.6.3.en: * "A faithful friend is the medicine of life" (Sir 6:16).

14.6.4.en: There is no remedy as effective in healing pains as the sincere righteous friend who comforts you in your afflictions, manages your problems, rejoices in your success and grieves in your calamities. He who has found such a friend has found a treasure. The faithful friend has no like, and the weight of gold and silver does not equal the goodness of his faithfulness [see (Sir 6:14-15)].

14.6.5.en: Truly, have a friend whom you call "half of my soul."

14.6.6.en: * There is no true friendship unless you make it like a joint that welds souls together, so that they cleave to one another by the love poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit.

14.6.7.en: St. Augustine * The strong is joined to the weak and supports him, and does not allow his destruction.

14.6.8.en: Again, if he is joined to a lazy person he raises him up and drives him to work. It is said: "A brother helped by a brother is a strong city." This is not surpassed by distance, nor heaven, nor earth, nor death, nor any other thing, but is stronger and more effective than all things. This, though it issues from one soul, is able to embrace many at once.

14.6.9.en: Hear what Paul says: "Ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels. Be ye also enlarged."

14.7.0.en: 8 The wisdom of the prudent is to understand his way: but the folly of fools is deceit. 9 Fools make a mock at sin: but among the righteous there is favour. 10 The heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy. 11 The house of the wicked shall be overthrown: but the tabernacle of the upright shall flourish. 12 There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.

14.7.1.en: "The wisdom of the prudent is to understand his way: but the folly of fools is deceit." [8]

14.7.2.en: The prudent man in wisdom knows his way and realizes his mission, but the fool deceives himself and does not know where he is going. The utmost kind of deceit is a man's deceiving himself. The fool thinks he knows everything and needs no helper to guide him, while he is ignorant even of himself. But the wise man, despite the wisdom given him, thirsts for the wisdom of God, and seeks it without ceasing, and respects the wisdom of others and values it with a spirit of discernment.

14.7.3.en: * "The wisdom of the able understands the ways of wisdom, and the folly of fools goes in the opposite direction." The prophecy says: [And to this man will I look, to him that is meek and quiet and trembleth at my words] (cf. Isa 66:2). We learn that there are three forms of friendship. The first and best is based on virtue, for the love that issues from reason is steadfast. The second stands midway between the two, its basis is reciprocity, where mutual sharing takes place and is useful for life. Friendship on the basis of free giving is reciprocity. The third and last we practice through habit. Some say that this form passes away and changes because it is founded on pleasure.

14.8.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria "Fools make a mock at sin: but among the righteous there is favour (grace)." [9]

14.8.1.en: Fools make light of sins, and drink them like water, and in heedlessness do not repent of what they commit. But the upright realize the value of their lives and feel the obligation, so they receive divine graces, and enjoy the blessings and are the object of God's pleasure and favor.

14.8.2.en: As an example of fools are those who carried Jeremiah off to Egypt, and persisted in worshiping idols, and when the Lord rebuked them by the mouth of the prophet, they said: "As for the word that thou hast spoken unto us in the name of the LORD, we will not hearken unto thee. But we will certainly do whatsoever thing goeth forth out of our own mouth, to burn incense unto the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto her, as we have done, we, and our fathers, our kings, and our princes, in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem: for then were we filled with bread, and were well, and saw no evil" (Jer 44:16-17). In folly they said that when they worshiped idols good things came upon them, and when they left them they came into want and were consumed by the sword and famine (Jer 44:18).

14.9.0.en: "The heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy." [10]

14.9.1.en: He who murmurs offers his heart bitterness, and he who rejoices offers it joy. It is as though what a man plants he eats of its fruit within him. The bitterness of the soul or its joy does not depend on the surrounding circumstances nor on the conduct of others, but on the conduct of the man himself.

14.9.2.en: A man often thinks he needs human consolations, but as righteous Job said through his bitter experience: "I have heard many such things: miserable comforters are ye all" (Job 16:2). For the distress and bitterness the heart carries cannot be escaped except by divine consolations, and the sweetness, joy and blessedness it carries will be understood by no one but himself! The psalmist says:

14.9.3.en: "In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul" (Ps 94:19).

14.9.4.en: "This is my comfort in my affliction: for thy word hath quickened me" (Ps 119:50).

14.9.5.en: "I remembered thy judgments of old, O LORD; and have comforted myself" (Ps 119:52).

14.9.6.en: "Let, I pray thee, thy merciful kindness be for my comfort, according to thy word unto thy servant" (Ps 119:76).

14.9.7.en: "As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem" (Isa 66:13).

14.9.8.en: "Therefore we, although we need none of these things, having for our comfort the holy books which are in our hands" (1 Macc 12:9).

14.9.9.en: "For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope" (Rom 15:4).

14.9.10.en: "Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort" (2 Cor 1:3).

14.9.11.en: "Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God" (2 Cor 1:4).

14.9.12.en: "For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ" (2 Cor 1:5).

14.9.13.en: * The multitude of trials that come upon us determines the greatness of our reward; as many as are the wounds that befall us, so many crowns we are made worthy of... If I shed one tear, I am made worthy of one consolation. If I shed ten tears, I am made worthy of ten consolations. The weight of my repentance is equal to the number of Your consolations.

14.9.14.en: St. Jerome * Reliance on men wholly prevents reliance on Christ, and outward consolation prevents hidden consolation.

14.10.0.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian "The house of the wicked shall be overthrown: but the tabernacle of the upright shall flourish." [11]

14.10.1.en: The wicked man thinks he is establishing for himself a stable and lasting house on earth, but it soon collapses with all its flimsy foundations; but the upright man, realizing that he is a stranger, sets up a tent in which he moves about, and yet his tent does not collapse but flourishes and his life grows without ceasing.

14.10.2.en: * I saw in the lower places a pit awaiting the wicked, and another place, different, prepared for the righteous.

14.11.0.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus "There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death." [12]

14.11.1.en: How easy it is for a man to deceive himself, and walk in a way that seems upright although its end is destruction.

14.11.2.en: * We read in Proverbs: "There is a way which seemeth right unto men, but the end thereof leads to the depths of hell." You see that ignorance too is clearly condemned in this text, where a man must think or else fall into hell, supposing that he has attained the truth. It says: [There are many devices in a man's heart] (cf. Prov 19:21). But it is not his wavering, doubtful and changeable will that prevails, but the counsel of God.

14.11.3.en: St. Jerome * When former sins come to your memory, flee from them as an upright, honorable man flees when he finds a wicked harlot seeking him on the public road, by her speaking to him or kissing him. For if he does not flee from her at once, lingering to talk with her in mixed conversations, even though he refuses to enjoy the shameful pleasure, he cannot avoid the contempt of the public and the mocking looks that rule over him. So we also, by this deadly remembering, fall into such thoughts. Therefore we must first refrain from holding to them, carrying out the commandment of Solomon, who says not to go there nor linger in her place, nor fix our gaze upon her, lest when the angels passing by see that we are occupied with unclean thoughts, they cannot say to us: "The blessing of the LORD be upon you" (Ps 129:8). For it is impossible for the mind to continue occupied with good things if the greater part of the heart is drowned in its wicked earthly meditations. Solomon's saying is indeed true: "Thine eyes shall behold strange women, and thine heart shall utter perverse things. Yea, thou shalt be as he that lieth down in the midst of the sea, or as he that lieth upon the top of a mast. They have stricken me, shalt thou say, and I was not sick; they have beaten me, and I knew it not" (Prov 23:33-35).

14.11.4.en: We must abandon not only evil thoughts but also thinking about temporal matters, lifting the longings of our souls toward heavenly things, as our Savior says: "Where I am, there shall also my servant be" (Jn 12:26). For it also happens, even out of sympathy, that we think of the falls or faults of others, and we are affected by pleasure and so fall into the cares of others. The result is that what we began well ends in a destructive end, because "There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death" (Prov 14:12).

14.12.s.en: 9. The joy and satisfaction of the heart

14.12.0.en: 13 Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness. 14 The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways: and a good man shall be satisfied from what he hath.

14.12.1.en: "Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness." [13]

14.12.2.en: Though God calls us to a life of true joy, issuing from the depths, He warns against laughter full of heedlessness, which is a cover for gloom of heart and inner bitterness. He who practices outward joy without an inward basis ends his joy in intense sorrow.

14.12.3.en: * If anyone wishes to ascend, let him not seek the joys of the world, its pleasures and delights, but what is painful and causes weeping, for to go to the house of mourning is better than to go to the house of feasting. Truly Adam would not have descended from Paradise had he not been deceived by pleasure.

14.12.4.en: St. Ambrose * The final end of human beings is to enter into a state of blessedness. If the Lord in the Gospel calls those who mourn blessed: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted" (Mt 5:4), then rightly He calls the end of every human being sorrow, for those who live in sorrow are filled from the overflow of spiritual blessings.

14.12.5.en: St. Evagrius * Where there is sorrow there are no formal behaviors (of joy). For love removes joy and laughter (on painful occasions). Sometimes we refrain from showing happiness out of consideration for those who are in sorrow or suffering pain. In the house of the feast the opposite happens: dancing and songs which cause shame, because they point to an uncontrolled life.

14.12.6.en: * Most people think it right to avoid the criticisms of the wise man, especially if they love sin. He who desires amusement and sin avoids him who prevents sin. He who lacks insight is pleased with flatterers, preferring flattery to criticism. It is a mark of the wise man to criticize the one he loves... Flatterers sing in a way. Even when they speak of morals they want to make their talk pleasing rather than useful. Such a song is a talk that offers joy, but rebuke helps a man to find the straight way.

14.12.7.en: * Thorns that burn under a pot give out loud crackling sounds. This is like the laughter of fools. It causes noise and crackling, and does not refine the soul... Just as thorns cause noise when burned like plants under a pot, in the same way the laughter of fools issues from an evil soul that is burning.

14.13.0.en: St. Didymus the Blind "The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways: and a good man shall be satisfied from what he hath." [14]

14.13.1.en: The backslider here differs from the apostate; the first is he who fails to attain knowledge because he relies on his own human understanding and wisdom, but the second has known the truth and yet rejects and denies it.

14.13.2.en: The backslider in heart is he who has put all his understanding on his heart (his mind) and so failed to attain the truth.

14.13.3.en: What a man does returns to him, so he who turns aside in his heart from the straight way, even if this does not appear openly in his outward conduct, is filled with the ways of his wicked heart, but the good man is satisfied with the goodness of his heart. It is as though a man does not eat from the hand of others, but from what his heart offers him.

14.14.0.en: 15 The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going. 16 A wise man feareth, and departeth from evil: but the fool rageth, and is confident.

14.14.1.en: "The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going." [15]

14.14.2.en: God created man a rational being, so that, lifting his mind toward God and seeking his sanctification, he may walk with understanding and wisdom in every step of his life, and not walk without aim.

14.14.3.en: The wise man calls us to enjoy a spirit of discernment and distinguishing, so that we do not walk without wisdom in our daily life and our dealings with others, and in our spiritual conduct.

14.14.4.en: * Through repentance we enter into His bliss by the grace of discernment that appears in us. He who lacks repentance is deprived of the bliss to come. He who is near to all is far from repentance, and he who withdraws from all with discernment is the truly penitent.

14.14.5.en: * By reading with discernment, gather your mind from everything and arise for prayer.

14.14.6.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian * Discernment is better than all the virtues.

14.14.7.en: The Spiritual Elder * I want you to be with the righteous. Hold fast to discernment like a helmsman, steering the ship according to the winds. And when you are sick, act according to your sickness in all the things about which I have written, and when you are well, act according to your health. For just as when the body is sick it does not accept food in its usual way, so also in this the rule shows that he is ailing.

14.14.8.en: St. Barsanuphius and his disciple John * An elder was asked: "How does a man find God, by fasting, by works, by watchfulness, or by mercy?" He said: "By all of these, surely, if they are mixed with discernment. Indeed I say that many tormented their bodies without discernment and then departed from us without gaining anything. Our mouths become foul from thirst, and we recite the Holy Scriptures with our mouths and pass through all the Psalms of David the prophet in our service, but what God requires and what is necessary we do not have, that is, the kind word from each of us to the other. For just as a man cannot see his face in troubled water, so the soul, if it is not purified from strange thoughts, cannot appear before God in prayer."

14.15.0.en: The Garden of the Monks "A wise man feareth, and departeth from evil: but the fool rageth, and is confident." [16]

14.15.1.en: Despite the courage and boldness before God that characterize the wise man, he fears error, and fears God and reveres Him. But the fool, despite the anxiety and lack of peace he carries within, is arrogant and rash. As someone said: "Fools rush in where angels fear to tread!" Thus in a spirit of discernment the wise man balances between confidence and boldness and the reverence fitting toward the Lord, but the fool in heedlessness carries no spirit of discernment and distinguishing.
